Marbled spinefoot Siganus rivulatus produces small, transparent pelagic eggs, with each fertilised ovum measuring 0.063 cm  in length, a dimension typical of siganid species that rely on widespread larval dispersal. At a rearing temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the embryos complete their development and undergo eclosion after approximately 30 hours , marking the emergence of the yolk-sac larva. This relatively rapid hatching period is consistent with other tropical marine teleosts and reflects the metabolic acceleration conferred by warm incubation conditions. Following chorion rupture, the prolarva remains endotrophic for a short interval, subsisting entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves before the mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences. The wet weight at birth, calculated from the assumed egg diameter, is roughly 0.000087 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.000087 grams], a minute mass that underscores the considerable energetic challenge facing early-stage larvae as they transition to planktivory in a resource-variable pelagic environment.

During the early developmental period at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the yolk-sac larva undergoes rapid morphological differentiation, achieving a total length at hatch of approximately 0.18 cm  immediately following eclosion. This modest size is characteristic of siganid larvae and necessitates a brief but critical yolk-dependent phase before the onset of first exogenous feeding. The age at birth for this species has been recorded at roughly 98 hours [ab = roughly 98 hours] after fertilisation when incubated at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], a duration that includes both the embryonic period and the initial yolk-sac stage prior to the completion of yolk absorption. Once the trophic switch is achieved, the actively growing larva enters a pelagic phase during which it feeds on small zooplankton. The relatively small hatchling length imposes a constraint on the prey spectrum available to the larva, limiting it largely to copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton during the first days of exogenous nutrition.

Juvenile Siganus rivulatus exhibit a prolonged growing phase as they transition from the pelagic larval habitat to benthic reef-associated environments. Field surveys indicate that individuals attain sexual maturation, marked by the onset of gonadal recrudescence, at a total length of 13.7 cm [Lp = 13.7 cm], with the corresponding wet weight at puberty averaging 31.3 grams [Wwp = 31.3 grams]. These values reflect the size thresholds necessary for reproductive activation in this species and are consistent with observations for other rabbitfishes in the Red Sea and eastern Mediterranean. The maximum recorded reproductive output for this species, measured under controlled conditions at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], is estimated at approximately 709,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 709,000 eggs per year] when averaged across the spawning season, representing a high fecundity typical of iteroparous broadcast spawners that compensate for low egg survivorship with substantial numerical output.

The ultimate total length attained by adult Siganus rivulatus is approximately 27 cm [Li = approximately 27 cm], while the asymptotic wet weight reaches roughly 350 grams [Wwi = roughly 350 grams], representing the maximum body size observed in wild populations. These values place the marbled spinefoot among the medium-sized members of the Siganidae, with a body plan well-suited to grazing on macroalgae in shallow coastal habitats. In terms of feeding physiology, laboratory trials conducted at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] have recorded a peak food intake rate of 0.051 grams per fish per day , a value that reflects the metabolic demands associated with sustained growth and reproduction under warm thermal regimes. This ingestion rate is comparable to those reported for other herbivorous reef fishes, which must process large volumes of low-nutrient algal material to meet their energetic requirements.

Maximum lifespan estimates for Siganus rivulatus, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age validation, indicate that individuals can survive for up to approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] under natural conditions at an average ambient temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This moderate longevity is typical of medium-sized rabbitfishes and reflects a life-history strategy that balances relatively rapid growth and early maturation against an extended reproductive window spanning several spawning seasons. Reproductive senescence has not been rigorously documented in this species, but field observations suggest that older individuals continue to participate in spawning aggregations alongside younger adults. The combination of high fecundity, broadcast spawning behaviour, and a multi-year reproductive lifespan contributes to the species' successful establishment as an invasive population in the Levantine Basin following its Lessepsian migration from the Red Sea.
